adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The growing demand for safer food and better nutritional and sensory quality creates the need for a better understanding of the processes involved in food production. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has been used by several authors for a better understanding of liquid food thermal process, one of the safest and most frequently used methods for food preservation. This study evaluated the condition of geometric symmetry used in numerical simulations of thermal process of packed liquid food via CFD. The analysis of temperature profiles obtained experimentally and through models built on 1/1, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and 1/32 of package geometry showed good correlation with the CFD simulations. The results indicate that the axial symmetry of the bottles allows the use of smaller models, which saves computational effort.</jats:p>

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The ability to measure all process variables is of great importance in the field of bioprocess monitoring and control, and continuous, real‐time measurements are highly desired. The more complete and real‐time the measurements are, the more stable, reproducible, and efficient the process can be, leading to reproducibly high‐quality products. This additional information allows the operator to better document the entire process. The process analytical technologies initiative of the US Food and Drug Administration is strongly related to the analysis and control of biopharmaceutical processes. The aim of the initiative is to create processes, generating products of ensured quality by measuring quality‐related process variables. The quality of the product is enhanced by a deep understanding of the process, which is enabled by an effective and suitable sensor system. The aim of this review is to provide an overview of current and emerging sensors for bioprocess monitoring. Sensors directly interfaced to bioreactors for measuring important variables from the gas phase, such as oxygen and carbon dioxide concentration, are discussed, as well as sensors for the monitoring of the biomass concentration and morphology and of the changing medium composition. Furthermore, sensor systems are discussed. These involve sensors (especially biosensors) that are not implemented directly inside the bioreactor but rather are used in conjunction with sample‐taking systems such as flow injection analysis. A major focus is given to spectroscopic sensors, which are noninvasive and offer interesting options for a simultaneous analysis of various compounds. Since data handling is extremely important for this kind of sensor, chemometrics are also included. Soft sensors are discussed as technology that allows a user to incorporate more process data as it become available. Finally, the current state of disposable sensor technology is presented. These sensors are needed for the growing area of disposable and continuous biomanufacturing.</jats:p>
title: Sensor systems for bioprocess monitoring

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>A modified bench scale calorimeter has been employed to determine the heat generated by various microbial strains growing on a range of different substrates, covering degrees of reduction from 3 to 6.13. The results are analyzed, and interpreted in the light of coupled enthalpy and elemental balances. The heat released by the microbial cultures has been found to correlate linearly with other process variables, such as biomass generation and oxygen uptake. The ratio between the heat generated and the biomass formed, the so‐called “heat yield” (<jats:italic>Y</jats:italic><jats:sub><jats:italic>Q/x</jats:italic></jats:sub>), has been shown both on theoretical and experimental grounds to increase with increasing degree of reduction of the substrate and to decrease with increasing biomass yield. The two effects could be combined into a simple model which permits the amount of heat released per unit of biomass formed to be predicted from the degree of reduction of the substrate as the only independent variable. The ratio between the heat generated and the oxygen taken up was constant at 440 kJ (mol O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>)<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup> throughout all experiments as expected from theoretical considerations for strongly aerobic processes.</jats:p>
title: Calorimetric investigation of aerobic fermentations

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:label/><jats:p>Storage tests were conducted to identify and compare factors influencing the growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. as specific spoilage organism on fresh pork and poultry. Besides the extrinsic factor, temperature, the intrinsic factors, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">pH</jats:styled-content>‐value, a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>‐value, Warner‐Bratzler shear force (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WBSF</jats:styled-content>), <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐glucose, L‐lactic acid, fat and protein content were analyzed. The growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. was clearly dependent on temperature, with faster growth at higher temperatures. Furthermore, growth was faster on fresh poultry than on fresh pork resulting in shorter shelf lives at constant temperatures from 2 to 15C. Almost all of the investigated intrinsic factors were significantly different (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.05) for fresh pork and poultry (except a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>‐value and L‐lactic acid). <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. counts correlated significantly to all investigated parameters in pork except <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WBSF</jats:styled-content> and to four of the seven parameters in poultry (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">pH</jats:styled-content>, a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>, <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐glucose, L‐lactic acid). However, magnitudes of these correlations were low, which indicates minor influences on shelf life.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Practical Applications</jats:title><jats:p>Early spoilage of fresh meat can lead to food waste and thereby economic losses as well as the loss of consumer confidence. Until now, there have been no previous detailed studies describing and comparing different intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and their influence on the growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. as specific spoilage organism in different types of meat. Understanding the main impact factors on shelf life of fresh pork and poultry is a prerequisite for the development of methods and tools for improving processes in meat supply chains. In particular, the results can serve as a basis for the development of mathematical models that can predict the shelf life and remaining shelf life of both meat types.</jats:p></jats:sec>
title: Characterization and Comparison of Spoilage Processes in Fresh Pork and Poultry

adjudicated_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The purpose of the present work is to present a review of literature on equations for fitting water sorption isotherms of foods and food products. Twenty-three equations, which have been proposed in the literature for correlating equilibrium moisture content in food systems, have been compiled and analysed. Their origin, range of applicability (both to type of food and water activity) and use are discussed. It is hoped that this critical compilation may be a useful guide for those researchers interested in the mathematical description of the water sorption isotherms of foods.</jats:p>
title: Equations for fitting water sorption isotherms of foods: Part 1 — a review

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The objective of this work was to apply Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to study the effect of particle orientation on fluid flow, temperature evolution, as well as microbial destruction, during thermal processing of still cans filled with peach halves in sugar syrup. A still metal can with four peach halves in 20% sugar syrup was heated at  100 °C for 20 min and thereafter cooled at 20 °C. Infinite heat transfer coefficient between heating medium and external can wall was considered. Peach halves were orderly placed inside the can with the empty space originally occupied by the kernel facing, in all peaches, either towards the top or the bottom of the can. In a third situation, the can was placed horizontally. Simulations revealed differences on particle temperature profiles, as well as process F values and critical point location, based on their orientation. At their critical points, peach halves with the kernel space facing towards the top of the can heated considerably slower and cooled faster than the peaches having their kernel space facing towards the bottom of the can. The horizontal can case exhibited intermediate cooling but the fastest heating rates and the highest F process values among the three cases examined. The results of this study could be used in designing of thermal processes with optimal product quality.</jats:p>
title: Effect of Particle Orientation during Thermal Processing of Canned Peach Halves: A CFD Simulation

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a theoretical model of situation awareness based on its role in dynamic human decision making in a variety of domains. Situation awareness is presented as a predominant concern in system operation, based on a descriptive view of decision making. The relationship between situation awareness and numerous individual and environmental factors is explored. Among these factors, attention and working memory are presented as critical factors limiting operators from acquiring and interpreting information from the environment to form situation awareness, and mental models and goal-directed behavior are hypothesized as important mechanisms for overcoming these limits. The impact of design features, workload, stress, system complexity, and automation on operator situation awareness is addressed, and a taxonomy of errors in situation awareness is introduced, based on the model presented. The model is used to generate design implications for enhancing operator situation awareness and future directions for situation awareness research.</jats:p>
title: Toward a Theory of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The growing consumer awareness of climate change and the resulting food sustainability issues have led to an increasing adoption of several emerging food trends. Some of these trends have been strengthened by the emergence of the fourth industrial revolution (or Industry 4.0), and its innovations and technologies that have fundamentally reshaped and transformed current strategies and prospects for food production and consumption patterns. In this review a general overview of the industrial revolutions through a food perspective will be provided. Then, the current knowledge base regarding consumer acceptance of eight traditional animal-proteins alternatives (e.g., plant-based foods and insects) and more recent trends (e.g., cell-cultured meat and 3D-printed foods) will be updated. A special focus will be given to the impact of digital technologies and other food Industry 4.0 innovations on the shift toward greener, healthier, and more sustainable diets. Emerging food trends have promising potential to promote nutritious and sustainable alternatives to animal-based products. This literature narrative review showed that plant-based foods are the largest portion of alternative proteins but intensive research is being done with other sources (notably the insects and cell-cultured animal products). Recent technological advances are likely to have significant roles in enhancing sensory and nutritional properties, improving consumer perception of these emerging foods. Thus, consumer acceptance and consumption of new foods are predicted to continue growing, although more effort should be made to make these food products more convenient, nutritious, and affordable, and to market them to consumers positively emphasizing their safety and benefits.</jats:p>
title: Consumer acceptance of new food trends resulting from the fourth industrial revolution technologies: A narrative review of literature and future perspectives

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The food industry faces many challenges, including the need to feed a growing population, food loss and waste, and inefficient production systems. To cope with those challenges, digital twins that create a digital representation of physical entities by integrating real-time and real-world data seem to be a promising approach. This paper aims to provide an overview of digital twin applications in the food industry and analyze their challenges and potentials. Therefore, a literature review is executed to examine digital twin applications in the food supply chain. The applications found are classified according to a taxonomy and key elements to implement digital twins are identified. Further, the challenges and potentials of digital twin applications in the food industry are discussed. The survey revealed that the application of digital twins mainly targets the production (agriculture) or the food processing stage. Nearly all applications are used for monitoring and many for prediction. However, only a small amount focuses on the integration in systems for autonomous control or providing recommendations to humans. The main challenges of implementing digital twins are combining multidisciplinary knowledge and providing enough data. Nevertheless, digital twins provide huge potentials, e.g., in determining food quality, traceability, or designing personalized foods.</jats:p>
title: Can a Byte Improve Our Bite? An Analysis of Digital Twins in the Food Industry

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>In the supply chain of perishable food products, large losses are incurred between farm and fork. Given the limited land resources and an ever-growing population, the food supply chain is faced with the challenge of increasing its handling efficiency and minimizing post-harvest food losses. Huge value can be added by optimizing warehouse management systems, taking into account the estimated remaining shelf life of the product, and matching it to the requirements of the subsequent part of the handling chain. This contribution focuses on how model approaches estimating quality changes and remaining shelf life can be combined in optimizing first-expired-first-out cold chain management strategies for perishable products. To this end, shelf-life-related performance indicators are used to introduce remaining shelf life and product quality in the cost function when optimizing the supply chain. A combinatorial exhaustive-search algorithm is shown to be feasible as the complexity of the optimization problem is sufficiently low for the size and properties of a typical commercial cold chain. The estimated shelf life distances for a particular batch can thus be taken as a guide to optimize logistics.</jats:p>
title: Shelf life modelling for first-expired-first-out warehouse management

titles.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions

descriptions.description: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The effect of uncertainty in thermal diffusivity on thermal process lethality was investigated for a model food of 8 percent canned bentonite suspension in two different can sizes. A developed computer program that account for can headspace thermal resistance and finite thermal resistance during cooling was used in this investigation. Six levels of errors in thermal diffusivity (±2%, ±5% and ±10%) were used to generate computer simulation time-temperature data at the geometric centre for both cans. The calculated lethality values from the time-temperature data when errors were imposed on thermal diffusivity were compared to that of the standard process. The results of the investigation revealed that error in thermal diffusivity of (-2%, -5% and -10%) resulted in under-processing, while error of (+2%, +5% and +10%) resulted in over processing. The magnitude of error in lethality from +10 percent errors in thermal diffusivity is substantial for both short can and long can investigated reaching a value of 35.4 percent for the short can and 44.5 percent for the tall can. The results from this study clearly indicate that thermal diffusivity could be a critical control point in thermal processing of foods which requires corrective action if there is deviation from the true value.</jats:p>
title: Numerical Investigation on the Effect of Uncertainty in Thermal Diffusivity on Thermal Process Lethality of Canned Foods

adjudicated_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
adjudicated_metadata.abstract: In the context of science, the well-known adage “a picture is worth a thousand words” might well be “a model is worth a thousand datasets.” Scientific models, such as Newtonian physics or biological gene regulatory networks, are human-driven simplifications of complex phenomena that serve as surrogates for the countless experiments that validated the models. Recently, machine learning has been able to overcome the inaccuracies of approximate modeling by directly learning the entire set of nonlinear interactions from data. However, without any predetermined structure from the scientific basis behind the problem, machine learning approaches are flexible but data-expensive, requiring large databases of homogeneous labeled training data. A central challenge is reconciling data that is at odds with simplified models without requiring "big data". In this work demonstrate how a mathematical object, which we denote universal differential equations (UDEs), can be utilized as a theoretical underpinning to a diverse array of problems in scientific machine learning to yield efficient algorithms and generalized approaches. The UDE model augments scientific models with machine-learnable structures for scientifically-based learning. We show how UDEs can be utilized to discover previously unknown governing equations, accurately extrapolate beyond the original data, and accelerate model simulation, all in a time and data-efficient manner. This advance is coupled with open-source software that allows for training UDEs which incorporate physical constraints, delayed interactions, implicitly-defined events, and intrinsic stochasticity in the model. Our examples show how a diverse set of computationally-difficult modeling issues across scientific disciplines, from automatically discovering biological mechanisms to accelerating the training of physics-informed neural networks and large-eddy simulations, can all be transformed into UDE training problems that are efficiently solved by a single software methodology.
title: Universal Differential Equations for Scientific Machine Learning

adjudicated_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>Ecological data often show temporal, spatial, hierarchical (random effects), or phylogenetic structure. Modern statistical approaches are increasingly accounting for such dependencies. However, when performing cross‐validation, these structures are regularly ignored, resulting in serious underestimation of predictive error. One cause for the poor performance of uncorrected (random) cross‐validation, noted often by modellers, are dependence structures in the data that persist as dependence structures in model residuals, violating the assumption of independence. Even more concerning, because often overlooked, is that structured data also provides ample opportunity for overfitting with non‐causal predictors. This problem can persist even if remedies such as autoregressive models, generalized least squares, or mixed models are used. Block cross‐validation, where data are split strategically rather than randomly, can address these issues. However, the blocking strategy must be carefully considered. Blocking in space, time, random effects or phylogenetic distance, while accounting for dependencies in the data, may also unwittingly induce extrapolations by restricting the ranges or combinations of predictor variables available for model training, thus overestimating interpolation errors. On the other hand, deliberate blocking in predictor space may also improve error estimates when extrapolation is the modelling goal. Here, we review the ecological literature on non‐random and blocked cross‐validation approaches. We also provide a series of simulations and case studies, in which we show that, for all instances tested, block cross‐validation is nearly universally more appropriate than random cross‐validation if the goal is predicting to new data or predictor space, or for selecting causal predictors. We recommend that block cross‐validation be used wherever dependence structures exist in a dataset, even if no correlation structure is visible in the fitted model residuals, or if the fitted models account for such correlations.</jats:p>
title: Cross‐validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure

descriptions.description: Conformal prediction is a technique for constructing prediction intervals that attain valid coverage in finite samples, without making distributional assumptions. Despite this appeal, existing conformal methods can be unnecessarily conservative because they form intervals of constant or weakly varying length across the input space. In this paper we propose a new method that is fully adaptive to heteroscedasticity. It combines conformal prediction with classical quantile regression, inheriting the advantages of both. We establish a theoretical guarantee of valid coverage, supplemented by extensive experiments on popular regression datasets. We compare the efficiency of conformalized quantile regression to other conformal methods, showing that our method tends to produce shorter intervals.

adjudicated_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Application of time temperature indicators (TTI) is based on response information or kinetic models from isothermal testing. The reliability of such models under variable temperature conditions was systematically studied. Nonisothermal experiments of two types were conducted involving prolonged exposures to high temperatures followed by storage at low temperatures to study the “history effect,” and storage at controlled, sinusoidaly varying temperatures. Three major types of commercial TTI were studied. Results showed that, although some types of TTI exhibit a significant “history effect,” the prediction models can be applied satisfactorily for the variable temperature storage.</jats:p>
title: Reliability of Time‐Temperature Indicators as Food Quality Monitors Under Nonisothermal Conditions

adjudicated_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>There is an urgent need to improve the infrastructure supporting the reuse of scholarly data. A diverse set of stakeholders—representing academia, industry, funding agencies, and scholarly publishers—have come together to design and jointly endorse a concise and measureable set of principles that we refer to as the FAIR Data Principles. The intent is that these may act as a guideline for those wishing to enhance the reusability of their data holdings. Distinct from peer initiatives that focus on the human scholar, the FAIR Principles put specific emphasis on enhancing the ability of machines to automatically find and use the data, in addition to supporting its reuse by individuals. This Comment is the first formal publication of the FAIR Principles, and includes the rationale behind them, and some exemplar implementations in the community.</jats:p>
title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The growing demand for safer food and better nutritional and sensory quality creates the need for a better understanding of the processes involved in food production. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has been used by several authors for a better understanding of liquid food thermal process, one of the safest and most frequently used methods for food preservation. This study evaluated the condition of geometric symmetry used in numerical simulations of thermal process of packed liquid food via CFD. The analysis of temperature profiles obtained experimentally and through models built on 1/1, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and 1/32 of package geometry showed good correlation with the CFD simulations. The results indicate that the axial symmetry of the bottles allows the use of smaller models, which saves computational effort.</jats:p>
title: Evaluation of Geometric Symmetry Condition in Numerical Simulations of Thermal Process of Packed Liquid Food by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD)

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The ability to measure all process variables is of great importance in the field of bioprocess monitoring and control, and continuous, real‐time measurements are highly desired. The more complete and real‐time the measurements are, the more stable, reproducible, and efficient the process can be, leading to reproducibly high‐quality products. This additional information allows the operator to better document the entire process. The process analytical technologies initiative of the US Food and Drug Administration is strongly related to the analysis and control of biopharmaceutical processes. The aim of the initiative is to create processes, generating products of ensured quality by measuring quality‐related process variables. The quality of the product is enhanced by a deep understanding of the process, which is enabled by an effective and suitable sensor system. The aim of this review is to provide an overview of current and emerging sensors for bioprocess monitoring. Sensors directly interfaced to bioreactors for measuring important variables from the gas phase, such as oxygen and carbon dioxide concentration, are discussed, as well as sensors for the monitoring of the biomass concentration and morphology and of the changing medium composition. Furthermore, sensor systems are discussed. These involve sensors (especially biosensors) that are not implemented directly inside the bioreactor but rather are used in conjunction with sample‐taking systems such as flow injection analysis. A major focus is given to spectroscopic sensors, which are noninvasive and offer interesting options for a simultaneous analysis of various compounds. Since data handling is extremely important for this kind of sensor, chemometrics are also included. Soft sensors are discussed as technology that allows a user to incorporate more process data as it become available. Finally, the current state of disposable sensor technology is presented. These sensors are needed for the growing area of disposable and continuous biomanufacturing.</jats:p>
title: Sensor systems for bioprocess monitoring

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>A modified bench scale calorimeter has been employed to determine the heat generated by various microbial strains growing on a range of different substrates, covering degrees of reduction from 3 to 6.13. The results are analyzed, and interpreted in the light of coupled enthalpy and elemental balances. The heat released by the microbial cultures has been found to correlate linearly with other process variables, such as biomass generation and oxygen uptake. The ratio between the heat generated and the biomass formed, the so‐called “heat yield” (<jats:italic>Y</jats:italic><jats:sub><jats:italic>Q/x</jats:italic></jats:sub>), has been shown both on theoretical and experimental grounds to increase with increasing degree of reduction of the substrate and to decrease with increasing biomass yield. The two effects could be combined into a simple model which permits the amount of heat released per unit of biomass formed to be predicted from the degree of reduction of the substrate as the only independent variable. The ratio between the heat generated and the oxygen taken up was constant at 440 kJ (mol O<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>)<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup> throughout all experiments as expected from theoretical considerations for strongly aerobic processes.</jats:p>

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:label/><jats:p>Storage tests were conducted to identify and compare factors influencing the growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. as specific spoilage organism on fresh pork and poultry. Besides the extrinsic factor, temperature, the intrinsic factors, <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">pH</jats:styled-content>‐value, a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>‐value, Warner‐Bratzler shear force (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WBSF</jats:styled-content>), <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐glucose, L‐lactic acid, fat and protein content were analyzed. The growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. was clearly dependent on temperature, with faster growth at higher temperatures. Furthermore, growth was faster on fresh poultry than on fresh pork resulting in shorter shelf lives at constant temperatures from 2 to 15C. Almost all of the investigated intrinsic factors were significantly different (<jats:italic>P</jats:italic> < 0.05) for fresh pork and poultry (except a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>‐value and L‐lactic acid). <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. counts correlated significantly to all investigated parameters in pork except <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">WBSF</jats:styled-content> and to four of the seven parameters in poultry (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">pH</jats:styled-content>, a<jats:sub>w</jats:sub>, <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>‐glucose, L‐lactic acid). However, magnitudes of these correlations were low, which indicates minor influences on shelf life.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Practical Applications</jats:title><jats:p>Early spoilage of fresh meat can lead to food waste and thereby economic losses as well as the loss of consumer confidence. Until now, there have been no previous detailed studies describing and comparing different intrinsic and extrinsic parameters and their influence on the growth of <jats:italic>Pseudomonas</jats:italic> spp. as specific spoilage organism in different types of meat. Understanding the main impact factors on shelf life of fresh pork and poultry is a prerequisite for the development of methods and tools for improving processes in meat supply chains. In particular, the results can serve as a basis for the development of mathematical models that can predict the shelf life and remaining shelf life of both meat types.</jats:p></jats:sec>
title: Characterization and Comparison of Spoilage Processes in Fresh Pork and Poultry

registered_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The purpose of the present work is to present a review of literature on equations for fitting water sorption isotherms of foods and food products. Twenty-three equations, which have been proposed in the literature for correlating equilibrium moisture content in food systems, have been compiled and analysed. Their origin, range of applicability (both to type of food and water activity) and use are discussed. It is hoped that this critical compilation may be a useful guide for those researchers interested in the mathematical description of the water sorption isotherms of foods.</jats:p>
title: Equations for fitting water sorption isotherms of foods: Part 1 — a review

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The objective of this work was to apply Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to study the effect of particle orientation on fluid flow, temperature evolution, as well as microbial destruction, during thermal processing of still cans filled with peach halves in sugar syrup. A still metal can with four peach halves in 20% sugar syrup was heated at  100 °C for 20 min and thereafter cooled at 20 °C. Infinite heat transfer coefficient between heating medium and external can wall was considered. Peach halves were orderly placed inside the can with the empty space originally occupied by the kernel facing, in all peaches, either towards the top or the bottom of the can. In a third situation, the can was placed horizontally. Simulations revealed differences on particle temperature profiles, as well as process F values and critical point location, based on their orientation. At their critical points, peach halves with the kernel space facing towards the top of the can heated considerably slower and cooled faster than the peaches having their kernel space facing towards the bottom of the can. The horizontal can case exhibited intermediate cooling but the fastest heating rates and the highest F process values among the three cases examined. The results of this study could be used in designing of thermal processes with optimal product quality.</jats:p>
title: Effect of Particle Orientation during Thermal Processing of Canned Peach Halves: A CFD Simulation

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a theoretical model of situation awareness based on its role in dynamic human decision making in a variety of domains. Situation awareness is presented as a predominant concern in system operation, based on a descriptive view of decision making. The relationship between situation awareness and numerous individual and environmental factors is explored. Among these factors, attention and working memory are presented as critical factors limiting operators from acquiring and interpreting information from the environment to form situation awareness, and mental models and goal-directed behavior are hypothesized as important mechanisms for overcoming these limits. The impact of design features, workload, stress, system complexity, and automation on operator situation awareness is addressed, and a taxonomy of errors in situation awareness is introduced, based on the model presented. The model is used to generate design implications for enhancing operator situation awareness and future directions for situation awareness research.</jats:p>

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The growing consumer awareness of climate change and the resulting food sustainability issues have led to an increasing adoption of several emerging food trends. Some of these trends have been strengthened by the emergence of the fourth industrial revolution (or Industry 4.0), and its innovations and technologies that have fundamentally reshaped and transformed current strategies and prospects for food production and consumption patterns. In this review a general overview of the industrial revolutions through a food perspective will be provided. Then, the current knowledge base regarding consumer acceptance of eight traditional animal-proteins alternatives (e.g., plant-based foods and insects) and more recent trends (e.g., cell-cultured meat and 3D-printed foods) will be updated. A special focus will be given to the impact of digital technologies and other food Industry 4.0 innovations on the shift toward greener, healthier, and more sustainable diets. Emerging food trends have promising potential to promote nutritious and sustainable alternatives to animal-based products. This literature narrative review showed that plant-based foods are the largest portion of alternative proteins but intensive research is being done with other sources (notably the insects and cell-cultured animal products). Recent technological advances are likely to have significant roles in enhancing sensory and nutritional properties, improving consumer perception of these emerging foods. Thus, consumer acceptance and consumption of new foods are predicted to continue growing, although more effort should be made to make these food products more convenient, nutritious, and affordable, and to market them to consumers positively emphasizing their safety and benefits.</jats:p>
title: Consumer acceptance of new food trends resulting from the fourth industrial revolution technologies: A narrative review of literature and future perspectives

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The food industry faces many challenges, including the need to feed a growing population, food loss and waste, and inefficient production systems. To cope with those challenges, digital twins that create a digital representation of physical entities by integrating real-time and real-world data seem to be a promising approach. This paper aims to provide an overview of digital twin applications in the food industry and analyze their challenges and potentials. Therefore, a literature review is executed to examine digital twin applications in the food supply chain. The applications found are classified according to a taxonomy and key elements to implement digital twins are identified. Further, the challenges and potentials of digital twin applications in the food industry are discussed. The survey revealed that the application of digital twins mainly targets the production (agriculture) or the food processing stage. Nearly all applications are used for monitoring and many for prediction. However, only a small amount focuses on the integration in systems for autonomous control or providing recommendations to humans. The main challenges of implementing digital twins are combining multidisciplinary knowledge and providing enough data. Nevertheless, digital twins provide huge potentials, e.g., in determining food quality, traceability, or designing personalized foods.</jats:p>

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>In the supply chain of perishable food products, large losses are incurred between farm and fork. Given the limited land resources and an ever-growing population, the food supply chain is faced with the challenge of increasing its handling efficiency and minimizing post-harvest food losses. Huge value can be added by optimizing warehouse management systems, taking into account the estimated remaining shelf life of the product, and matching it to the requirements of the subsequent part of the handling chain. This contribution focuses on how model approaches estimating quality changes and remaining shelf life can be combined in optimizing first-expired-first-out cold chain management strategies for perishable products. To this end, shelf-life-related performance indicators are used to introduce remaining shelf life and product quality in the cost function when optimizing the supply chain. A combinatorial exhaustive-search algorithm is shown to be feasible as the complexity of the optimization problem is sufficiently low for the size and properties of a typical commercial cold chain. The estimated shelf life distances for a particular batch can thus be taken as a guide to optimize logistics.</jats:p>
title: Shelf life modelling for first-expired-first-out warehouse management

titles.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions

descriptions.description: Understanding why a model makes a certain prediction can be as crucial as the prediction's accuracy in many applications. However, the highest accuracy for large modern datasets is often achieved by complex models that even experts struggle to interpret, such as ensemble or deep learning models, creating a tension between accuracy and interpretability. In response, various methods have recently been proposed to help users interpret the predictions of complex models, but it is often unclear how these methods are related and when one method is preferable over another. To address this problem, we present a unified framework for interpreting predictions, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP assigns each feature an importance value for a particular prediction. Its novel components include: (1) the identification of a new class of additive feature importance measures, and (2) theoretical results showing there is a unique solution in this class with a set of desirable properties. The new class unifies six existing methods, notable because several recent methods in the class lack the proposed desirable properties. Based on insights from this unification, we present new methods that show improved computational performance and/or better consistency with human intuition than previous approaches.

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>The effect of uncertainty in thermal diffusivity on thermal process lethality was investigated for a model food of 8 percent canned bentonite suspension in two different can sizes. A developed computer program that account for can headspace thermal resistance and finite thermal resistance during cooling was used in this investigation. Six levels of errors in thermal diffusivity (±2%, ±5% and ±10%) were used to generate computer simulation time-temperature data at the geometric centre for both cans. The calculated lethality values from the time-temperature data when errors were imposed on thermal diffusivity were compared to that of the standard process. The results of the investigation revealed that error in thermal diffusivity of (-2%, -5% and -10%) resulted in under-processing, while error of (+2%, +5% and +10%) resulted in over processing. The magnitude of error in lethality from +10 percent errors in thermal diffusivity is substantial for both short can and long can investigated reaching a value of 35.4 percent for the short can and 44.5 percent for the tall can. The results from this study clearly indicate that thermal diffusivity could be a critical control point in thermal processing of foods which requires corrective action if there is deviation from the true value.</jats:p>

registered_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
registered_metadata.abstract: In the context of science, the well-known adage “a picture is worth a thousand words” might well be “a model is worth a thousand datasets.” Scientific models, such as Newtonian physics or biological gene regulatory networks, are human-driven simplifications of complex phenomena that serve as surrogates for the countless experiments that validated the models. Recently, machine learning has been able to overcome the inaccuracies of approximate modeling by directly learning the entire set of nonlinear interactions from data. However, without any predetermined structure from the scientific basis behind the problem, machine learning approaches are flexible but data-expensive, requiring large databases of homogeneous labeled training data. A central challenge is reconciling data that is at odds with simplified models without requiring "big data". In this work demonstrate how a mathematical object, which we denote universal differential equations (UDEs), can be utilized as a theoretical underpinning to a diverse array of problems in scientific machine learning to yield efficient algorithms and generalized approaches. The UDE model augments scientific models with machine-learnable structures for scientifically-based learning. We show how UDEs can be utilized to discover previously unknown governing equations, accurately extrapolate beyond the original data, and accelerate model simulation, all in a time and data-efficient manner. This advance is coupled with open-source software that allows for training UDEs which incorporate physical constraints, delayed interactions, implicitly-defined events, and intrinsic stochasticity in the model. Our examples show how a diverse set of computationally-difficult modeling issues across scientific disciplines, from automatically discovering biological mechanisms to accelerating the training of physics-informed neural networks and large-eddy simulations, can all be transformed into UDE training problems that are efficiently solved by a single software methodology.
title: Universal Differential Equations for Scientific Machine Learning

decisions.original_reference: Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., Boyce, M. S., Elith, J., & Guillera‐Arroita, G. (2017). Cross‐validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881

decisions.corrected_reference: Roberts, D. R., Bahn, V., Ciuti, S., Boyce, M. S., Elith, J., Guillera‐Arroita, G., Hauenstein, S., Lahoz‐Monfort, J. J., Schröder, B., Thuiller, W., Warton, D. I., Wintle, B. A., Hartig, F., & Dormann, C. F. (2017). Cross‐validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography, 40(8), 913-929. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecog.02881

registered_metadata.abstract: <jats:p>Ecological data often show temporal, spatial, hierarchical (random effects), or phylogenetic structure. Modern statistical approaches are increasingly accounting for such dependencies. However, when performing cross‐validation, these structures are regularly ignored, resulting in serious underestimation of predictive error. One cause for the poor performance of uncorrected (random) cross‐validation, noted often by modellers, are dependence structures in the data that persist as dependence structures in model residuals, violating the assumption of independence. Even more concerning, because often overlooked, is that structured data also provides ample opportunity for overfitting with non‐causal predictors. This problem can persist even if remedies such as autoregressive models, generalized least squares, or mixed models are used. Block cross‐validation, where data are split strategically rather than randomly, can address these issues. However, the blocking strategy must be carefully considered. Blocking in space, time, random effects or phylogenetic distance, while accounting for dependencies in the data, may also unwittingly induce extrapolations by restricting the ranges or combinations of predictor variables available for model training, thus overestimating interpolation errors. On the other hand, deliberate blocking in predictor space may also improve error estimates when extrapolation is the modelling goal. Here, we review the ecological literature on non‐random and blocked cross‐validation approaches. We also provide a series of simulations and case studies, in which we show that, for all instances tested, block cross‐validation is nearly universally more appropriate than random cross‐validation if the goal is predicting to new data or predictor space, or for selecting causal predictors. We recommend that block cross‐validation be used wherever dependence structures exist in a dataset, even if no correlation structure is visible in the fitted model residuals, or if the fitted models account for such correlations.</jats:p>
title: Cross‐validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure

descriptions.description: Conformal prediction is a technique for constructing prediction intervals that attain valid coverage in finite samples, without making distributional assumptions. Despite this appeal, existing conformal methods can be unnecessarily conservative because they form intervals of constant or weakly varying length across the input space. In this paper we propose a new method that is fully adaptive to heteroscedasticity. It combines conformal prediction with classical quantile regression, inheriting the advantages of both. We establish a theoretical guarantee of valid coverage, supplemented by extensive experiments on popular regression datasets. We compare the efficiency of conformalized quantile regression to other conformal methods, showing that our method tends to produce shorter intervals.

registered_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Application of time temperature indicators (TTI) is based on response information or kinetic models from isothermal testing. The reliability of such models under variable temperature conditions was systematically studied. Nonisothermal experiments of two types were conducted involving prolonged exposures to high temperatures followed by storage at low temperatures to study the “history effect,” and storage at controlled, sinusoidaly varying temperatures. Three major types of commercial TTI were studied. Results showed that, although some types of TTI exhibit a significant “history effect,” the prediction models can be applied satisfactorily for the variable temperature storage.</jats:p>
title: Reliability of Time‐Temperature Indicators as Food Quality Monitors Under Nonisothermal Conditions

registered_metadata.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>There is an urgent need to improve the infrastructure supporting the reuse of scholarly data. A diverse set of stakeholders—representing academia, industry, funding agencies, and scholarly publishers—have come together to design and jointly endorse a concise and measureable set of principles that we refer to as the FAIR Data Principles. The intent is that these may act as a guideline for those wishing to enhance the reusability of their data holdings. Distinct from peer initiatives that focus on the human scholar, the FAIR Principles put specific emphasis on enhancing the ability of machines to automatically find and use the data, in addition to supporting its reuse by individuals. This Comment is the first formal publication of the FAIR Principles, and includes the rationale behind them, and some exemplar implementations in the community.</jats:p>
title: The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship

ALGORITHM 1.1: Closed-Loop Execution and VVUQ Fallback Protocol of the
               Six-Layer Trustworthy Food Digital Twin (TFDT / TFPDT-RA)
INPUTS:
  - Validated physical sensor & PAT telemetry stream y_raw(t_k) from Layer 1;
  - Prior twin state-parameter distribution p(x_D(t_{k-1}^+), theta_D(t_{k-1}^+));
  - Hybrid physics-informed evolution operator F_D(x_D, u_P; theta_D) (Layer 3);
  -Metrological covariance R_k, OOD threshold chi^2_{n_y, 1-beta}, and statutory
   food safety bound L_crit (with target confidence 1 - alpha).

OUTPUTS:
  - Posterior state & quality/safety distributions p(x_D(t_k^+)), p(Psi_safety(t_k));
  - Verified actuation command u_cmd(t_k) (Layer 5 optimal or Layer 6 safe fallback);
  - Mechanistic/SHAP explanation vector Phi_explain(t_k) and PROV-DM audit record.
1. FOR each discrete synchronisation step k = 1, 2, ..., K_batch DO:

   2.1. Layer 1 & Layer 2 (Telemetry Acquisition & Data Reliability Gate - Alg. 3.1):
        a. Acquire multi-rate physical and PAT measurements y_raw(t_k) (Layer 1).
        b. Perform IEEE 1588 clock alignment and RTD Lagrangian mapping (Layer 2).
        c. Screen for sensor faults via PCA T^2/Q-residuals; assign metrological
           uncertainty covariance R_k (JCGM GUM) and compute DQI_k.
        d. IF sensor fault detected on non-redundant safety channel THEN:
              Trigger hardware PLC alarm; set Twin_Status = SENSOR_FAULT; GOTO 2.5(b).

   2.2. Layer 3 (Hybrid Physics-Informed Forecast & Bayesian Assimilation - Alg. 5.1):
        a. Propagate ensemble/sigma-points of (x_D(t_{k-1}^+), theta_D(t_{k-1}^+))
           through reduced-order PDE/kinetic core F_D = f_mech + r_ML over [t_{k-1}, t_k].
        b. Verify thermodynamic invariants (mass/energy balance, dS_irr >= 0, a_w in [0,1]).
        c. Compute innovation nu_k = y_val(t_k) - H_D(x_hat_D(t_k^-)) and innovation
           covariance S_k = H_k P_k^- H_k^T + R_k; update posterior p(x_D(t_k^+), theta_D(t_k^+)).

   2.3. Layer 4 (Predictive Quality/Safety, Conformal Bounds & Three-Tier OOD Gate - Alg. 8.2):
        a. Propagate posterior state to evaluate Remaining Shelf Life RSL_{1-alpha}(t_k),
           cold-spot lethality F_{0,LB}^{(1-alpha)}(t_k), and 2D QMRA pathogen risk.
        b. Evaluate Mahalanobis distance d_M^2(t_k) = nu_k^T S_k^{-1} nu_k, spectral
           Q-residual, and ensemble epistemic spread Tr(P_k^+).
        c. IF d_M^2(t_k) <= chi^2_{n_y, 1-beta} AND Tr(P_k^+) <= sigma^2_max THEN:
              Set Twin_Status = TRUSTWORTHY_NOMINAL.
           ELSE:
              Set Twin_Status = OOD_DRIFT_WARNING; flag epistemic abstention.

   2.4. Layer 5 (Risk-Constrained Multi-Objective eNMPC & CBF-QP Safety Shield - Alg. 7.1, 9.2):
        a. IF Twin_Status == TRUSTWORTHY_NOMINAL THEN:
              Solve chance-constrained multi-objective eNMPC over horizon [t_k, t_k + T_p]:
                 u_MPC*(t_k) = argmin_u J_Pareto(Quality, Yield, Exergy, Cost)
                 subject to: P(Psi_safety(t) >= L_crit) >= 1 - alpha.
              Filter u_MPC*(t_k) through Zeroing CBF-QP safety shield -> u_cmd(t_k).

   2.5. Layer 6 (Human-in-the-Loop Governance, Fallback & Audit Trail - Alg. 7.2, 13.1):
        a. IF Twin_Status == TRUSTWORTHY_NOMINAL THEN:
              Transmit u_cmd(t_k) to Layer 1 PLC/DCS; render SHAP attribution Phi_explain(t_k).
        b. ELSE (Twin_Status == OOD_DRIFT_WARNING or SENSOR_FAULT):
              ABSTAIN from ML-assisted optimisation; switch actuator command to
              pre-validated conservative HACCP/mechanistic trajectory:
                 u_cmd(t_k) = u_HACCP_safe(t_k).
              Issue Explainable Alert to Human Operator and TwinOps drift registry.
        c. Append cryptographically signed record {t_k, y_val, x_hat_k^+, R_k,
           Twin_Status, u_cmd, Phi_explain} to immutable W3C PROV-DM / 21 CFR Part 11 ledger.
3. END FOR

ALGORITHM 2.1: Coupled Multiphase Porous Transport, Thermodynamic State, and
               Non-Isothermal Kinetic Solver (Layer 3 Mechanistic Engine)
Inputs at step k:
  - Previous state fields at t_{k-1}: T^{k-1}(r), S_w^{k-1}(r), rho_v^{k-1}(r),
    P_g^{k-1}(r), u_s^{k-1}(r), C_i^{k-1}(r), log10_N^{k-1}(r), F_0^{k-1}(r)
  - Assimilated parameter vector from Layer 3: theta_k = [k_eff, K_w, D_va, ...]
  - Boundary actuation & fluid states over [t_{k-1}, t_k]: u(t), T_inf(t), RH_inf(t)
Outputs at step k:
  - Updated state fields x_d(t_k), algebraic states z_alg(t_k), predicted sensor
    outputs y_hat(t_k), and quality/safety/exergy KPIs q_KPI(t_k)
1: // STEP 1: Mesh & Poromechanical Geometry Update (Lagrangian-Eulerian ALE)
2: FOR each spatial element / REV node m = 1 ... N_nodes DO
3:     Compute dry-basis moisture X_w,m = (phi_m * S_w,m * rho_w) / ((1 - phi_m)*rho_s)
4:     Evaluate Gordon-Taylor glass transition T_g,m(X_w,m) via Eq. (2.11)
5:     Compute the WLF shift factor for viscosity or relaxation time via Eq. (2.12); evaluate E_m from a separately specified constitutive model.
6: END FOR
7: Solve quasi-static poromechanical momentum balance (Eq. 2.6) for displacement u_s^k
   and solid skeleton velocity v_s^k = (u_s^k - u_s^{k-1}) / Delta_t; update porosity phi^k.

8: // STEP 2: Implicit Newton-Raphson Solution of Coupled Heat & Mass PDEs
9: Initialise Newton iterate l = 0 with U^{(0)} = [T^{k-1}, S_w^{k-1}, rho_v^{k-1}, P_g^{k-1}]
10: REPEAT
11:    FOR each spatial node m = 1 ... N_nodes DO
12:        Evaluate GAB / Flory-Huggins water activity a_w,m(T^{(l)}, X_w^{(l)}) (Eq. 2.9)
13:        Evaluate net isosteric heat q_st,m(X_w^{(l)}) and Delta_H_vap,m (Eq. 2.10)
14:        Evaluate non-equilibrium evaporation source I_evap,m^{(l)} (Eq. 2.8)
15:        Evaluate Darcy-Fick fluxes n_{w,rel}^{(l)}, n_{v,rel}^{(l)} (Eq. 2.4a-2.4c)
16:        IF electromagnetic heating active THEN
17:            Update dielectric properties eps''(T^{(l)}, X_w^{(l)}) and solve Maxwell/Helmholtz
               equation for volumetric source q_dot_EM,m^{(l)}
18:        END IF
19:    END FOR
20:    Evaluate conjugate Robin boundary fluxes at moving surface dOmega(t_k) (Eq. 2.7a-2.7b)
21:    Assemble global residual vector R(U^{(l)}) and Jacobian matrix J = dR/dU for
       mass conservation (Eq. 2.2-2.3) and energy conservation (Eq. 2.5)
22:    Solve linear system J * Delta_U^{(l)} = -R(U^{(l)}); update U^{(l+1)} = U^{(l)} + Delta_U^{(l)}
23:    Increment l <- l + 1
24: UNTIL ||Delta_U^{(l)}||_2 / ||U^{(l)}||_2 < tol_NR (e.g., 10^{-6})
25: Set converged transport states: [T^k, S_w^k, rho_v^k, P_g^k] <- U^{(l)}

26: // STEP 3: Non-Isothermal Differential Integration of Quality & Safety Kinetics
27: FOR each spatial node m = 1 ... N_nodes (and Lagrangian particle trajectories) DO
28:     Integrate physicochemical quality ODEs (Eq. 2.13-2.14) over [t_{k-1}, t_k]
        using 4th-order Runge-Kutta / Radau IIA to obtain C_{i,m}^k
29:     IF T_m^k >= T_lethal_min (Thermal Inactivation Regime) THEN
30:         Integrate differential Weibull (Eq. 2.16) or Geeraerd (Eq. 2.17) survival ODE
            for log10(N_m^k / N_0)
31:         Update cumulative lethality F_{0,m}^k = F_{0,m}^{k-1} + integral_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}
            10^{(T_m(tau) - T_ref)/z_T} d_tau (Eq. 2.19)
32:     ELSE IF T_min < T_m^k < T_max (Biokinetic Growth Regime) THEN
33:         Integrate Baranyi-Roberts dynamic growth & physiological state ODEs
            (Eq. 2.18a-2.18b) for N_m^k and intracellular bottleneck q_m^k
34:     END IF
35: END FOR

36: // STEP 4: Macroscopic Conservation Check, Exergy Audit & KPI Extraction
37: Verify integral macroscopic fluid-solid mass/energy closure (Eq. 2.20)
38: Compute instantaneous exergy destruction rate Ex_dot_dest(t_k) = T_0 * S_dot_gen(t_k)
    via Eq. (2.22) and exergetic efficiency psi_ex(t_k) via Eq. (2.23)
39: Extract cold-spot safety lethality F_proc(t_k) = min_m F_{0,m}^k, volume-averaged
    quality bar_C_i(t_k), and predicted sensor vector y_hat(t_k) = H(x_d^k, z_alg^k)
40: RETURN x_d(t_k), z_alg(t_k), y_hat(t_k), q_KPI(t_k)
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 2.1. Coupled Multiphase Porous Transport, Thermodynamic State, and Reaction Kinetics Solver.

ALGORITHM 3.1: Automated Pre-Modelling Data Readiness and Reliability Gate
               (Layer 1 → Layer 2/3 Qualification Protocol)
INPUTS:
  - Raw multi-rate sensor & PAT stream y_raw(t), flow rate V_dot(t), ISA-88 Phase
  - Metrological GUM uncertainty parameters {u_cal, u_drift, u_trans, u_chem}
  - Calibration reference subspace {mu_MCD, Sigma_MCD, P_PCA, Lambda_PCA, Q_alpha, T2_alpha}
  - Calibration transfer matrices {F_PDS, b_PDS} and RTD kernel E(tau; Pe_L, V_dot)
  - Reference feature sample X^(0) for Kernel MMD drift detection & FIM threshold kappa_max

OUTPUTS:
  - Validated, Lagrangian-aligned observation vector y_val,k
  - Dynamic observation error covariance matrix R_k (GUM + drift-inflated)
  - Composite Data Quality Index DQI_k in [0, 1] and Twin Operating Mode Flag
  - Tamper-evident W3C PROV-DM lineage node e_ValidatedObs_k with SHA-256 hash h_k

PROCEDURE:
1. SOURCE CLOCK & ANTI-ALIASED MULTI-RATE ALIGNMENT:
   a. Verify IEEE 1588 PTP / NTP source timestamp t_gen,k; flag packet if clock offset > Delta_t_max.
   b. Apply strictly causal FIR anti-aliasing decimation filter (Eq. 3.22) to fast PLC channels.
   c. If offline LIMS assay y_lab(t_sample) arrives at t_report > t_sample:
        Route y_lab to historical state buffer at epoch t_sample for OOSM retrodiction.

2. SPECTRAL PRE-PROCESSING & CALIBRATION TRANSFER (FOR PAT CHANNELS):
   a. Apply strictly causal one-sided Savitzky–Golay derivative filter (Eq. 3.16) and SNV (Eq. 3.17).
   b. Standardise secondary probe spectra to master domain via PDS (Eq. 3.12):
        x_tilde_k^T <- x_S,k^T * F_PDS + b_PDS^T
   c. Project onto PLS latent scores (Eq. 3.8) and evaluate GUM covariance Sigma_z,k (Eq. 3.9–3.10).

3. ROBUST SUBSPACE FAULT ISOLATION VS PHYSICAL PROCESS EXCURSION:
   a. Standardise vector z_k using robust MCD parameters (mu_MCD, Sigma_MCD).
   b. Compute Hotelling's T2_k (Eq. 3.19) and Q-residual Q_k (Eq. 3.20).
   c. IF Q_k <= Q_alpha AND T2_k <= T2_alpha THEN:
        Mode <- NORMAL_NOC; retain all channels.
      ELSE IF Q_k <= Q_alpha AND T2_k > T2_alpha THEN:
        Mode <- PHYSICAL_PROCESS_EXCURSION;
        // CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: Never delete as outlier! Pass immediately to Twin CCP engine.
        Retain all channels; flag high-priority safety assimilation.
      ELSE IF Q_k > Q_alpha AND T2_k <= T2_alpha THEN:
        Mode <- ISOLATED_SENSOR_FAULT;
        Identify faulty channel j* = argmax_j c^Q_{k,j} (Eq. 3.21).
        Mask channel j* via selection matrix S_k; reconstruct via variable-dimension Kalman filter;
        Trigger automated probe air-purge / maintenance ticket if PAT channel.
      ELSE (Q_k > Q_alpha AND T2_k > T2_alpha):
        Mode <- COMPOUND_FAULT_OR_OUT_OF_MANIFOLD;
        Inflate R_k <- gamma_inflate * Sigma_z,k; switch Twin to First-Principles PDE Fallback.

4. LAGRANGIAN RESIDENCE-TIME CONVOLUTION (CONTINUOUS LINES) OR DTW (BATCH):
   a. Convolve upstream inlet measurements u_in(t) with axial RTD kernel E(tau; Pe_L, V_dot(t))
      via Eq. (3.24) to align material parcels at downstream sensor coordinate L.

5. DISTRIBUTIONAL DRIFT & IDENTIFIABILITY GATE:
   a. Compute sliding-window PSI (Eq. 3.29), 1-Wasserstein distance W_1 (Eq. 3.30),
      and Kernel MMD^2 (Eq. 3.31) against reference calibration distribution P_0.
   b. If in Offline Model Calibration Mode:
        Assemble scaled Fisher Information Matrix F_tilde(theta) (Eq. 3.32);
        IF kappa_FIM(F_tilde) > kappa_max (Eq. 3.34) THEN:
          ABORT parameter fitting; issue D-Optimal Experimental Design excitation request.

6. COMPOSITE DQI EVALUATION & CRYPTOGRAPHIC PROVENANCE COMMIT:
   a. Compute sub-indices (q_comp, q_metro, q_sub, q_sync, q_drift) and geometric DQI_k (Eq. 3.35).
   b. Generate W3C PROV-DM entity e_ValidatedObs_k (Eq. 3.26) and append SHA-256 hash chain h_k (Eq. 3.27).
   c. Return (y_val,k, R_k, DQI_k, Mode, h_k) to Layer 3 Hybrid Digital Twin State Observer.
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 3.1. Automated Pre-Modelling Data Readiness and Reliability Gate

ALGORITHM 4.1: Identifiability-Audited Hybrid Grey-Box Calibration and Selection
Input:  Batch-grouped dataset D = {B_1, ..., B_G} passing Algorithm 3.1 Gate;
        Mechanistic conservation operator F_mech(x, u; θ_mech);
        Candidate hybrid closure g_ML(x, u; w) with hard bounding layer ψ_bound;
        Measurement covariance matrices {Σ_k} from GUM audit (Chapter 3).
Output: Verified parameter vector θ*, posterior covariance/intervals [θ_min, θ_max],
        trained hybrid closure g_ML*, and Applicability Domain threshold γ_crit.

1. REPARAMETERISATION & STRUCTURAL AUDIT:
   a. Apply reference-temperature centring T_ref = mean(T) to all Arrhenius/Peleg
      rate laws to reduce numerical correlation between the Arrhenius parameters; this does not resolve structural non-identifiability.
   b. Verify local structural identifiability rank(∂Y/∂θ_mech) = n_θ at nominal
      trajectories; if rank-deficient, lump non-identifiable parameters.

2. STAGE 1 — MECHANISTIC BACKBONE CALIBRATION & PROFILE LIKELIHOOD:
   a. Solve global-local NLLS (Eq. 4.15) via Enhanced Scatter Search + Levenberg-
      Marquardt using forward sensitivity ODEs (Eq. 4.16-4.17) to obtain θ_mech*.
   b. Compute Fisher Information Matrix I(θ_mech*) (Eq. 4.19) and condition number κ(I).
   c. For each parameter i = 1 to n_θ:
        Compute 1D Profile Likelihood PL(θ_i) (Eq. 4.21) across [0.1 θ_i*, 10 θ_i*].
        If PL(θ_i) fails to cross 2 Φ_NLLS(θ*) + χ²_{1, 0.95}:
           Flag θ_i as PRACTICALLY NON-IDENTIFIABLE; either fix θ_i to literature
           prior (Rao, 2014) or generate E-Optimal Dynamic Design u*(t).

3. STAGE 2 — PHYSICS-CONSTRAINED GREY-BOX CLOSURE TRAINING:
   a. Freeze identifiable mechanistic parameters θ_mech* (or use as Bayesian prior).
   b. Embed bounded closure θ_const = ψ_bound(g_ML(x, u; w)) inside F_mech (Eq. 4.34)
      or train GPR residual compensator Δy_GPR(x_mech, u) on residuals e_k (Eq. 4.35).
   c. Evaluate Group K-Fold Cross-Validation RMSEP_group across unseen batches B_g.

4. STAGE 3 — EXTRAPOLATION STRESS TEST & APPLICABILITY GATE:
   a. Evaluate candidate model on out-of-hull stress grid (T ± 15 °C, X ± 20%):
      Verify zero mass-balance violation (||m^T dx/dt|| = 0) and strict monotonicity
      of thermal lethality (dF_0/dt >= 0).
   b. Set runtime applicability gate: if γ_GPR(x_*) = σ_GPR²(x_*)/σ_f² > γ_crit,
      attenuate ML correction weight to zero and fall back to F_mech(x, u; θ_mech*).
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 4.1: Iterative Profile-Likelihood Identifiability Audit and Physics-Constrained Grey-Box Parameter Estimation.

algorithms.source_text:
ALGORITHM 5.1: TFDT / TFPDT-RA Real-Time State Synchronisation, Prediction, and Supervision
Input:  Prior assimilated belief state (x_hat_{k-1|k-1}, θ_hat_{k-1|k-1}, P_{k-1|k-1});
        Validated inline sensor vector y_fast,k and PAT spectrum s_k at t_k = k Δt_sync;
        Applied actuator input u_{k-1}; CUSUM state S_{CUSUM,k-1}.
Output: Updated belief state (x_hat_{k|k}, θ_hat_{k|k}, P_{k|k});
        Terminal quality & safety distribution q_hat(t_f) ± z_{1-α/2} σ_q(t_f);
        Verified supervisory setpoint u_k* and Twin Health Status Flag.

1. LAYERS 1 & 2 — SENSING, METROLOGICAL DATA GATE & PAT COVARIANCE (Chapters 2-3):
   a. Acquire Layer 1 telemetry and execute Layer 2 Algorithm 3.1; obtain aligned y_fast,k and GUM R_{fast,k}.
   b. Project PAT spectrum s_k -> y_{PAT,k}; compute Hotelling T²_k and Q_{res,k}.
   c. Inflate PAT measurement covariance R_{PAT,k} via Eq. (5.39) if Q_{res,k} > Q_α.
   d. Assemble composite measurement y_k = [y_{fast,k}; y_{PAT,k}], R_k = blkdiag(R_fast, R_PAT).

2. LAYER 3 (PART A) — DETERMINISTIC HYBRID DAE PREDICTION STEP (Chapter 4):
   a. Evaluate applicability domain ratio γ_GPR(x_hat_{k-1|k-1}) = σ_GPR² / σ_f².
   b. If γ_GPR > γ_crit: attenuate hybrid ML residual weight to zero (mechanistic fallback).
   c. Generate 2(n_x + n_θ) + 1 augmented sigma points X_{i,k-1} (Eq. 5.13) [or MHE grid].
   d. Integrate each sigma point over [t_{k-1}, t_k] using fixed-step L-stable RODAS
      solver (Eq. 5.43-5.44) coupled to the Thermodynamic Property Server.
   e. Compute a priori state-parameter mean x_tilde_{k|k-1} and covariance P_{k|k-1} (Eq. 5.14).

3. LAYER 3 (PART B) — CONSTRAINED STATE-PARAMETER ASSIMILATION (Chapter 5):
   a. Compute predicted observation y_hat_{k|k-1}, innovation e_k = y_k - y_hat_{k|k-1},
      innovation covariance S_k (Eq. 5.15), and Kalman gain K_k = P_{xy,k} S_k^-1 (Eq. 5.16).
   b. Compute unconstrained update x_tilde_{k|k}^uncon = x_tilde_{k|k-1} + K_k e_k.
   c. Apply Simon's covariance-weighted projection (Eq. 5.41a-5.41b) onto physical
      conservation & positivity manifold Ω = {C_cons x = d_k, x >= 0, θ ∈ [θ_min, θ_max]}.
   d. If a delayed LIMS assay y_slow(t_{k_s}) arrived at t_k: invoke Algorithm 5.2.

4. LAYER 4 — SELF-AUDITING VV&UQ DRIFT GATE & FORWARD QUALITY/SAFETY ROLLOUT (Chapters 6-8):
   a. Compute Normalised Innovation Squared ε_{NIS,k} = e_k^T S_k^-1 e_k (Eq. 5.5) and
      update Page-Hinkley CUSUM statistic S_{CUSUM,k} (Eq. 5.28).
   b. Propagate sigma points of N(x_hat_{k|k}, P_{k|k}) forward over remaining horizon
      [t_k, t_f] at 100x real-time to compute terminal quality q_hat(t_f), microbial
      lethality F_0(t_f), and upper/lower credible bounds Σ_{q}(t_f).

5. LAYERS 5 & 6 — RISK-AWARE SUPERVISORY CONTROL, SAFETY SHIELD & HITL GOVERNANCE (Chapters 9-13):
   a. If S_{CUSUM,k} > h_CUSUM or WCET > 0.8 Δt_sync:
        Hold nominal PLC setpoints; issue Layer 6 Operator XAI & Re-Calibration Alert.
   b. Else:
        Solve chance-constrained NMPC problem enforcing P(F_0(t_f) >= F_{0,min}) >= 1 - δ
        to obtain optimal setpoint u_k*; log provenance and transmit u_k* + heartbeat to PLC (Tier 0).
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 5.1: Trustworthy Food Process Digital Twin Reference Architecture (TFDT / TFPDT-RA) Master Real-Time Synchronisation and Supervision Cycle.

algorithms.source_text:
ALGORITHM 5.2: Exact Multi-Rate Assimilation of Time-Delayed Laboratory Assays
Input:  Delayed assay measurement y_slow(t_{k_s}) with sampling timestamp t_{k_s},
        arrival timestamp t_{k_a} = t_{k_s} + D Δt_sync, and GUM covariance R_slow;
        Ring buffer entry {x_tilde_{k_s|k_s}, P_{k_s|k_s}, Φ_tilde_{k_a, k_s}} (Eq. 5.33).
Output: Corrected current state-parameter estimate x_tilde_{k_a|k_a}^corr and P_{k_a|k_a}^corr.

1. Retrieve historical snapshot x_tilde_{k_s|k_s}, P_{k_s|k_s} at sampling step k_s.
2. Evaluate slow observation map h_slow(x_tilde_{k_s|k_s}) and Jacobian H_{slow, k_s}.
3. Compute historical innovation e_{slow, k_s} = y_slow(t_{k_s}) - h_slow(x_tilde_{k_s|k_s})
   and innovation covariance S_{slow, k_a} = H_{slow, k_s} P_{k_s|k_s} H_{slow, k_s}^T + R_slow.
4. Gate outlier: if e_{slow, k_s}^T S_{slow, k_a}^-1 e_{slow, k_s} > χ²_{n_slow, 0.999}, reject assay.
5. Compute extrapolated cross-covariance gain K_{slow, k_a} = Φ_tilde_{k_a, k_s} P_{k_s|k_s} H_{slow, k_s}^T S_{slow, k_a}^-1 (Eq. 5.34).
6. Apply state-parameter correction x_tilde_{k_a|k_a}^corr (Eq. 5.35) and covariance reduction
   P_{k_a|k_a}^corr (Eq. 5.36), followed by conservation projection P_Ω (Eq. 5.41).
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 5.2: Asynchronous Delayed-Measurement State and Parameter Correction for At-Line / LIMS Assays.

ALGORITHM 6.1: Real-Time Cold-Chain Digital Twin Assimilation, Spatial Thermal Reconstruction, and Stochastic Remaining Shelf Life (RSL) Estimation
INPUTS:
  - Pallet ID b, intake covariate vector z_b, and population NLME hyperparameters (beta_fixed, Z_cov, Omega_batch, R_eps)
  - Reduced-order porous-media pallet thermal matrices (A_therm(u_air), B_therm(u_air)) across N_z spatial zones (surface, intermediate, core)
  - Coupled packaging-kinetic ODE/DAE system f_q(q, T, RH, p_O2, p_CO2, theta) and sensory survival threshold parameters (eta_s, beta_s, p_rej*)
  - Real-time IoT telemetry packet at step t_k: ambient air temperature T_air,k, relative humidity RH_amb,k, airflow state u_air,k, and optional headspace/PAT reading y_PAT,k
  - Future supply-chain route scenario parameters (expected transit time tau_trans,d, stochastic ambient temperature process e_future(tau))

OUTPUTS:
  - Spatial quality state distribution {q_hat_{z,k|k}, P_{q,z,k|k}} for each pallet zone z = 1..N_z
  - Pallet-level conservative Remaining Shelf Life prediction bound RSL_0.05(t_k), median RSL_0.50(t_k), and Dynamic FEFO routing assignment

STEP 1: INITIALISATION AT PALLET INTAKE (k = 0)
  1.1 Compute prior batch kinetic & initial-state distribution via Eq. (6.32b):
        phi_hat_{b,0|0} <- beta_fixed + Z_cov * z_b
        P_{phi,b,0|0}   <- Omega_batch
  1.2 Compute critical acceptability vector q_crit from sensory Weibull survival cutoff (Eq. 6.30):
        q_crit <- q_0 + eta_s * [ -ln(1 - p_rej*) ]^(1 / beta_s)

STEP 2: SPATIAL THERMAL & PACKAGING MASS-BALANCE RECONSTRUCTION OVER [t_{k-1}, t_k]
  2.1 Validate incoming IoT telemetry (T_air,k, RH_amb,k) through Chapter 3 Gross Error Detection (GED) gate.
  2.2 Integrate reduced-order porous-media heat & moisture balance (with internal respiration heat Q_resp(T_z)) across zones z = 1..N_z:
        T_hat_{z,k} <- Propagate_ROM_Thermal(T_hat_{z,k-1}, T_air,k, RH_amb,k, u_air,k, dt_k)
  2.3 For each zone z, update package moisture X_{w,z,k}, water activity a_{w,z,k} (Eqs. 6.18-6.19), and headspace gas partial pressures (p_{O2,z,k}, p_{CO2,z,k}) (Eq. 6.20).

STEP 3: MULTI-PATHWAY QUALITY KINETICS & BAYESIAN OBSERVER UPDATE
  3.1 For each pallet zone z = 1..N_z, integrate coupled physical, chemical, and SSO microbial differential equations (Eqs. 6.8-6.25, 6.39) over [t_{k-1}, t_k] using L-stable Rosenbrock-Wanner step:
        q_hat_{z,k|k-1}, P_{q,z,k|k-1} <- CD_EKF_or_UKF_Predict(q_hat_{z,k-1|k-1}, P_{q,z,k-1|k-1}, T_hat_{z,k}, a_{w,z,k}, p_{O2,z,k}, p_{CO2,z,k}, phi_hat_{b,k-1})
  3.2 IF an inline/at-line PAT or headspace sensor measurement y_PAT,k is available at t_k:
        Update state and batch random effects b_b via Empirical Bayes / Kalman update (Eqs. 6.33-6.34):
        q_hat_{z,k|k}, P_{q,z,k|k}, phi_hat_{b,k|k}, P_{phi,b,k|k} <- Kalman_Measurement_Update(q_hat_{z,k|k-1}, y_PAT,k, R_eps)
      ELSE:
        q_hat_{z,k|k} <- q_hat_{z,k|k-1} ; P_{q,z,k|k} <- P_{q,z,k|k-1}

STEP 4: STOCHASTIC FORWARD ROLLOUT FOR FIRST-PASSAGE RSL DISTRIBUTION
  4.1 Identify the worst-case (limiting) spatial zone z* = argmax_z { Fault_Proximity(q_hat_{z,k|k}, q_crit) } (e.g., warmest zone for microbial growth; highest-light/O2 exterior zone for photo-oxidation).
  4.2 Draw N_ens Monte Carlo / Unscented ensemble realizations {q_k^(i), phi_b^(i)} from N(q_hat_{z*,k|k}, P_{q,z*,k|k}) and N(phi_hat_{b,k|k}, P_{phi,b,k|k}).
  4.3 Propagate each realization i = 1..N_ens forward over future horizon tau > 0 under reference or route-specific temperature scenario e_future^(i)(t_k + tau) until boundary crossing:
        tau_RSL^(i) <- inf { tau > 0 : g_{q,j}(q^(i)(t_k + tau)) > 0 for any limiting attribute j = 1..m_q }
  4.4 Sort {tau_RSL^(1), ..., tau_RSL^(N_ens)} to extract empirical quantiles:
        RSL_0.05(t_k) <- Quantile_0.05({tau_RSL^(i)})
        RSL_0.50(t_k) <- Quantile_0.50({tau_RSL^(i)})

STEP 5: DYNAMIC FEFO LOGISTICS INTERLOCK
  5.1 Evaluate route failure risk P_fail,d = Count(tau_RSL^(i) < tau_trans,d + tau_disp,d) / N_ens for each candidate destination d.
  5.2 Solve Dynamic FEFO assignment (Eq. 6.43) and publish (RSL_0.05(t_k), RSL_0.50(t_k), Limiting_Pathway_ID) to Warehouse Management System (WMS).
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 6.1: Dynamic Cold-Chain Digital Twin State Updating and Stochastic RSL Computation

algorithms.source_text:
ALGORITHM 6.2: Online Shelf-Life Attribution and Constrained Counterfactual Intervention Synthesis
INPUTS:
  - Assimilated batch trajectory {q_hat(tau), e(tau)} over tau in [0, t_k] across logistics stages s = 1..N_stage
  - Current posterior state (q_hat_{k|k}, P_{q,k|k}), batch feature vector z_feat,k, and predicted (RSL_0.05(t_k), RSL_0.50(t_k))
  - Commercial shelf-life requirement RSL_target and feasible environmental control bounds [u_min, u_max] (including chilling injury limit T_chill,min)

OUTPUTS:
  - Stage-wise shelf-life consumption vector Phi_stage[1..N_stage]
  - Reaction pathway attribution vector pi_path[1..R_path]
  - Batch-specific Shapley explanation vector phi_SHAP[1..d_f]
  - Optimal counterfactual intervention Delta_u_env* (if RSL_0.05(t_k) < RSL_target)

STEP 1: STAGE-WISE & PATHWAY DEGRADATION ATTRIBUTION
  1.1 For each completed processing/logistics stage s = 1..N_stage over [t_{s-1}, t_s]:
        Phi_stage[s] <- Integral_{t_{s-1}}^{t_s} |dq(tau)/dtau| dtau / |q_crit - q_0|   (Eq. 6.48a)
  1.2 For each parallel reaction pathway r = 1..R_path of the limiting quality attribute j*:
        Flux_cum[r]  <- Integral_0^{t_k} S_{j*,r} * r_r(q_hat(tau), e(tau)) dtau
  1.3 Normalise pathway contributions:
        pi_path[r]   <- Flux_cum[r] / Sum_{m=1}^{R_path} Flux_cum[m]                     (Eq. 6.48b)

STEP 2: FEATURE-LEVEL SHAPLEY DECOMPOSITION
  2.1 Evaluate conditional expectations v(S) = E[RSL_0.50 | Z_S = z_S,k] over population NLME prior distribution.
  2.2 Compute exact or interventional Shapley attributions phi_SHAP[i] for i = 1..d_f via Eq. (6.50a).
  2.3 Verify exact additivity check:
        | Sum_{i=1}^{d_f} phi_SHAP[i] - (RSL_0.50(t_k) - E_pop[RSL_0.50]) | < 10^-6

STEP 3: COUNTERFACTUAL PRESCRIPTION GENERATION (IF RSL PREDICTION BOUND IS BELOW TARGET)
  3.1 IF RSL_0.05(t_k) < RSL_target:
        Formulate constrained NLP (Eq. 6.50b) over controllable future variables Delta_u_env = [Delta_T_set, Delta_RH_set, Delta_tau_trans]^T:
          Minimise   || W_u * Delta_u_env ||_2^2
          Subject to RSL_0.05(q_hat_{k|k}, u_env,k + Delta_u_env) >= RSL_target
                     max(u_min, T_chill,min) <= u_env,k + Delta_u_env <= u_max
        Solve NLP via Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) using analytical adjoint sensitivities d(RSL_0.05)/du_env.
        IF feasible solution Delta_u_env* exists:
          Issue actionable prescription (Delta_T_set*, Delta_tau_trans*) to HMI and WMS FEFO router.
        ELSE:
          Flag batch for immediate local clearance / secondary processing before quality boundary breach.
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 6.2. Mechanistic Pathway Attribution, SHAP Decomposition, and Counterfactual Shelf-Life Prescription

algorithms.source_text: ALGORITHM 7.1: Sampled supervisory barrier filter. Inputs: validated telemetry, estimated state and covariance, nominal control, actuator limits, and a declared risk model. (1) Reject stale or invalid telemetry and propagate the process and uncertainty models. (2) Evaluate physical hazard margins and, only when its assumptions hold, the sampled back-off in Equation (7.49). (3) Solve the actuator-constrained QP within a monitored deadline, including any required inter-sample tightening. (4) Check solver residuals, feasibility, command acknowledgement, and applicability of the uncertainty model. (5) On any failed check, freeze supervisory writes and execute the independently validated diversion, quarantine, or shutdown procedure. (6) Log the model version, assumptions, margins, solution status, actual actuator response, and affected product window. Output: a model-screened command or a fallback request; no unconditional safety certificate is returned.
algorithms.caption: Algorithm 7.1: Real-Time Dynamic Critical Control Point (dCCP) Observer and CBF-QP Safety Shield
